title: Paying Engineers like Salespeople – Arman Hezarkhani, Tenex

primary.label: AI Product, UX & Human Factors

summary: Arman Hezarkhani, co-founder and managing partner at Tenex, introduces a compensation model where engineers are paid like salespeople—based on story points completed rather than hours worked. Clients are charged per story point delivered, and engineers receive a flat base salary plus quarterly compensation tied to completed story points. He motivates this by recounting a WeWork experience where an adjacent engineer typed code character by character while he ran 45 AI agents simultaneously, attributing the divergence to incentives rather than capability. He traces a brief history of compensation: hourly (disincentivizes speed and encourages overestimation), salary plus bonus (encourages clock-watching), and equity (effective but risky and not universally appealing). He argues these models must be reinvented for the AI age to directly incentivize tool adoption and high-quality output. Tenex operates in two modes: roadmapping and execution. Strategists—mostly technical former PMs and engineers—distill client requirements and scope tickets; AI engineers produce architecture design documents broken into tickets graded by story points. The two roles create a counterbalance: strategists are compensated based on NRR (customer happiness), and every ticket requires multiple rounds of QA plus client approval. Arman then addresses key risks: story point inflation (mitigated by strategists scoping work), quality drops from rushing (mitigated by QA and client sign-off), and sharp-elbowed sales-like culture (mitigated by rigorous hiring). He emphasizes that Tenex makes hiring intentionally difficult so everything else becomes easy, quoting co-founder Alex that AI is like a funhouse mirror—it amplifies whatever attributes an engineer already has. He closes by inviting the audience to rethink compensation models to unlock employee potential, regardless of domain. Two case studies anchor the talk: a billboard company AI moderation model built in two weeks at 96% accuracy versus human moderators, and a retail device company where Tenex delivered five parallel on-device models spanning heat mapping, queue detection, theft detection, and more.

sections.title: Introduction and Premise
sections.summary: Arman introduces himself as co-founder at Tenex and states the core thesis: they pay engineers like salespeople, based on story points completed. He notes skepticism from distinguished engineers but claims the model has enabled hiring elite talent and shipping high-quality code rapidly.

sections.title: The WeWork Story and the Incentive Problem
sections.summary: Arman recounts seeing a fellow WeWork engineer typing code character by character while he ran 45 AI agents. He attributes the gap not to skill but to incentives: as a founder he sought maximum efficiency, while a salaried employee with annual bonus and equity lacks the same drive to adopt AI tooling.

sections.title: Brief History of Compensation
sections.summary: Arman traces compensation evolution: hourly (disincentivizes speed, encourages overestimation), salary plus bonus (encourages clock-watching), and equity (effective for startups but risky and not universally appealing). He argues the model must be reinvented for the AI era to directly incentivize tool adoption and quality.

sections.title: How Tenex's Model Works
sections.summary: Tenex does roadmapping and execution. Strategists (mostly technical former PMs/engineers) distill client requirements. AI engineers produce architecture design documents—the bulk of engineering time—then implement tickets graded by story points. Engineers receive a flat base plus quarterly payment for completed story points.

sections.title: Client Project Examples
sections.summary: Two case studies: a billboard company where Tenex built an AI content moderation model in two weeks at 96% accuracy versus human moderators, and a retail device company where Tenex identified new model opportunities and built five models running in parallel on low-power edge devices covering heat mapping, queue detection, theft detection, and more.

sections.title: Risks, Mitigations, and Closing
sections.summary: Arman addresses key risks: story point inflation, quality drops from rushing, and sharp-elbowed sales-like culture. Mitigations include the two-role counterbalance (strategists compensated on NRR scope the work, engineers paid per story point), multiple QA rounds plus client approval on every ticket, and intentionally difficult hiring. He quotes co-founder Alex that AI amplifies existing attributes like a funhouse mirror. He closes by inviting the audience to rethink compensation to unlock employee potential and provides his contact.

demonstrations: Billboard company AI moderation model replacing two rounds of human moderation, built in two weeks at 96% accuracy compared to human moderators
Retail device company: five models running in parallel on low-power devices covering heat mapping, queue detection, theft detection, and more
limitations: The talk is presented as a perspective, not a prescription—Arman explicitly states his goal is not to convince everyone to adopt the model
The brief history of compensation is described as illustrative rather than accurate
The model depends heavily on rigorous hiring, which Arman acknowledges as intentionally difficult
